lessons.title: Build Rust with an explicit edition
lessons.summary: After editing the message, you run the previous executable without rebuilding. What can appear?
explanation: rustc translates a Rust source file into an executable. Editing main.rs does not change an already-built executable.
This course uses stable Rust 1.99.1 with edition 2024. An edition is not the same thing as a compiler version; one compiler can support several editions.
Cargo reads a manifest named Cargo.toml. The early single-file examples can also be compiled directly with rustc.
These fixtures need no downloaded crates or nightly features. The app shows concepts and checks rather than a Rust browser runner.
Expected output or behavior: Ready. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: In a new folder save main.rs, run rustc --edition=2024 main.rs -o lesson, then ./lesson. Compare running before and after rebuilding an edited message. You may trace it without a Rust compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.

lessons.title: Numeric types and inferred values
lessons.summary: Replace both operands with 5.0 and 2.0. What prints?
explanation: u8 holds unsigned whole numbers from 0 through 255. i32 is a signed 32-bit type; usize is an unsigned size/index type whose width follows the target.
A suffix such as 3u8 selects a type explicitly. Without other constraints, an integer variable commonly defaults to i32.
f64 represents approximate fractions with finite precision. A numeric type is not a guarantee that every real-world quantity fits exactly.
5 /2 uses integer division. 5.0 /2.0 uses floating-point division; Rust does not implicitly mix an integer variable with a floating one.
Expected output or behavior: 2. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Compare explicit small integer and floating calculations. Name the types rather than assuming a variable can hold every number. You may trace it without a Rust compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.

lessons.title: Checked integer arithmetic
lessons.summary: Change the added amount from 10 to 3. What prints?
explanation: Ordinary integer overflow can panic when overflow checks are enabled and can behave differently with other compilation settings. Do not use build settings as an implicit validation policy.

The dot in value.checked_add(10) selects a method on value; the parentheses supply the added amount. For u8, checked_add returns Some(result) if the sum fits and None if it does not. These are explicit success/absence variants; later lessons develop Option fully.
{:?} asks for a Debug representation. It displays Some(253) or None here, unlike an ordinary numeric display.
The example uses checked_add, so its behavior does not depend on whether ordinary overflow checks were enabled.
Expected output or behavior: None. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

explanation: value as i32 converts a primitive numeric value to i32. It is not a text parser.

lessons.title: Boolean short-circuit conditions
lessons.summary: Set denominator to 0. What prints?
explanation: Rust conditions require Boolean expressions; a nonzero integer is not automatically a true condition.
&& skips its right operand when the left is false. || skips its right operand when the left is true.
The denominator check comes before division. A zero denominator makes the left side false and prevents evaluation of the division.
Short-circuiting determines which operations run, not just the final Boolean.
Expected output or behavior: true. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Characters strings and UTF-8
lessons.summary: Change the text to "A". What prints?
explanation: A single-quoted char such as 'é' is a Unicode scalar value, not merely one UTF-8 byte and not a complete grapheme cluster in every case.
String::from("é") creates an owned growable String. A double-quoted string literal provides an &str borrowed text view; full borrowing rules follow later.
String.len counts UTF-8 bytes. chars().count counts Unicode scalar values. Neither is a universal count of user-perceived characters.
The sample é uses two UTF-8 bytes and one scalar value. ASCII A uses one byte and one scalar value.
Expected output or behavior: 2 1. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Loop values and control
lessons.summary: Change the break value to 9. What prints?
explanation: loop has no condition of its own. break exits it; continuing forever is not useful merely because it compiles.
break 7 sends 7 out of the loop expression. The surrounding let can store that result.
The body reaches break on its first pass, so no timing or overflow assumption is needed.
for visits a sequence and while repeats while a Boolean remains true. This lesson isolates the value-producing loop form.
Expected output or behavior: 7. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Functions and expression results
lessons.summary: Add a semicolon after value*2 in the function body without adding return. What happens?

value*2 without a trailing semicolon is the block’s result expression.
Adding a semicolon turns that expression into a statement; the block would then return unit (), which does not match this i32 signature.
return value*2; exits with that value. This example uses the final-expression style.

lessons.title: Ownership and scope
lessons.summary: Move the text print after the closing brace. What happens?
explanation: Ownership determines who is responsible for a value and when its resources are released. When an owner goes out of scope, its value is dropped unless ownership has moved.
A binding declared inside a block is not available outside that block.
An owned String controls heap-backed text as well as its local binding. The principle is about responsibility, not simply where bytes live.
This example prints the String inside its owning scope, then continues after the block.

lessons.title: Exclusive mutable borrowing
lessons.summary: Change the starting score to 7. What prints?
explanation: &mut score creates a mutable reference. Through that reference, *value designates the original i32 for assignment. *value += 1 adds one and stores the result back through that reference.
let mut score makes the original binding mutable so it may be mutably borrowed.
You cannot keep simultaneously usable conflicting shared and mutable borrows of the same data. The rule prevents unsynchronized conflicting access in safe Rust.
A function without an explicit return type returns unit (). It performs its update through the borrowed reference.
Expected output or behavior: 4. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Borrow lifetimes and last use
lessons.summary: Move text.push before the print of view. What happens?
explanation: The compiler can determine that a shared borrow is no longer used after its final access. Its effective restriction need not last to the closing brace.
Here view is printed before text.push, so the shared borrow is no longer needed when mutation begins.
If text.push occurs before a later print of view, the mutable access overlaps a still-needed shared borrow and is rejected.
No runtime borrow counter is used for these ordinary references. Later RefCell has a different runtime-checked mechanism.

lessons.title: Growable vectors
lessons.summary: Remove the push call. What length prints?
explanation: vec![2,4] constructs a vector of elements. Unlike a fixed array, its length can change.
let mut values permits push to append an element. len returns the current number of elements.
A vector may reserve more storage than currently initialized elements. Only valid indices below len can be read.
Rust prevents growing a vector while an incompatible live reference to one of its elements is still being used.

lessons.title: Slices and borrowed views
lessons.summary: Change the borrowed range to 0..2. What prints?
explanation: The slice type [T] describes a contiguous sequence; &[T] is a borrowed reference to it. &values[1..3] borrows elements at indices 1 and 2, excluding 3, without owning a copied collection.
view[0] refers to the original values[1], because the view starts one position into the array.
The slice reference remains tied to the underlying array’s valid lifetime.
The start and end must describe a valid range. An invalid checked range panics rather than creating arbitrary storage.

lessons.title: Option and explicit absence
lessons.summary: Change the initializer to None. What prints?
explanation: Option<T> is either Some(value) or None. The type parameter T names the kind of value that may be present.
match examines the variant. Each arm uses pattern => result, and commas separate arms. Some(value) binds the payload; None selects the absence branch.
This program deliberately maps absence to 0. Other tasks may need to report missing data instead.
unwrap would panic on None. Matching lets the program handle absence without assuming it away.

lessons.title: Result and explicit failure
lessons.summary: Replace Ok(7) with Err(String::from("missing")). What prints?
explanation: Result<T,E> contains Ok(value) or Err(error). T and E are the success and error types.
match binds the successful value or error payload. This example uses a String as the error message.
Constructing Err does not unwind the program. The surrounding code chooses how to handle or propagate it.
Real operations often provide structured error types. A String here keeps the initial success/failure distinction visible.
